title: Stability hardening for speculative kernel probing and rate smoothing
creator: Aisha Khan
content:
Summary:

During a capacity surge on 2026-02-16 we observed repeated short-lived regressions in P95/P99 latency across a subset of medium-length text workloads. The root cause was an interaction between the speculative kernel probing logic in the scheduler and a recently deployed rate-smoothing change that inadvertently amplified probe-induced churn. This ticket captures the post-incident follow-up, mitigations, and tracked action items.

Context and observed behavior:
- Systems affected: hosted inference pools serving gpt-like and opt-variant models in us-west-2.
- Symptoms: multi-minute windows of elevated tail latency and increased token-cost due to repeated kernel recompiles/reshuffles.
- Timeline: surge began ~2026-02-16T03:12Z; first alerts at 03:18Z; automated fallback engaged at 03:32Z; manual mitigation rolled at 04:05Z.
- Scope: ~12% of requests for the affected model family experienced p95 > 250 ms (baseline ~120 ms) with p99 spikes up to 600 ms. KV cache warmup variance increased p95 by an additional ~30ms in cold-paths.

Root cause (summary):
1) Speculative kernel probing: the scheduler probes alternate optimized kernels when path-affinity metrics drop. Probes are designed to be lightweight but were allowed to occur at high frequency under bursty arrival patterns.
2) Rate-smoothing change: a late-stage change (ENG-449890) introduced a more aggressive request-rate smoothing window to reduce oscillation during normal traffic. Under high burstiness this smoothing delayed the scheduler's convergence signal, causing multiple overlapped probes rather than suppressing them.
3) Probe amplification loop: overlapped probes increased short-term resource contention (memory and compilation slots), which in turn caused more requests to fall into nonoptimal paths and trigger further probing — an amplification feedback loop leading to transient kernel thrashing and elevated per-token latency.
4) Secondary factors: KV cache miss variance and autotuner sensitivity to sequence-length histograms increased the probability of probe selection in mid-length workloads.

Immediate mitigations (what we did):
- Rolled back the aggressive rate-smoothing change (hotfix) at 2026-02-16T04:05Z which reduced probe overlap and restored baseline tail latency. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8214)
- Disabled speculative probe execution concurrency beyond 1 slot per worker as a temporary guard.
- Enabled a conservative kernel blacklist timer (30s) to avoid immediate retries on a recently-failed kernel.
- Notified on-call and customer success for high-touch customers in the affected regions.

Analysis and metrics collected:
- Traces and flamegraphs captured from the affected period are stored in the incident dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/incident-2026-02-16-kernel-probe
- Probe frequency histogram before/after rollback shows 4x reduction in concurrent probes per worker.
- Compilation queue depth and memory pressure metrics spiked during the incident; post-mitigation they return to baseline within 10 minutes.
- Regression impact matrix attached: drive link: https://drive.redwood.ai/incident-reports/ENG-450001/postmortem.pdf

Decision points and trade-offs considered:
- Conservative short-term rollback vs. throttled probe pacing: we chose rollback to avoid prolonged tail risk while we design a safer probe pacing algorithm.
- Blacklisting duration: 30s chosen as conservative starting point to reduce immediate flapping; longer durations risk preventing useful kernel migration under real workload shifts.
- Probe scheduling granularity: shifting to centralized probe gating would add complexity but offers stronger global coordination; we plan a phased approach starting with local pacing.

Action plan (owner, estimate, due):
1) Implement probe backoff and jitter (local pacing): reduce probe attempts per-worker and add exponential backoff + random jitter. Owner: Priya Patel. Estimate: 5 pts. Due: 2026-03-22.
2) Add global probe rate controller in scheduler to limit cluster-wide concurrent probes during high concurrency events. Owner: Marcus Lee. Estimate: 8 pts. Due: 2026-04-05.
3) Improve telemetry: emit per-kernel probe counters, probe duration histograms, and probe-failure reasons. Instrumentation ticket: ENG-455678. Owner: Noah Diaz. Estimate: 3 pts. Due: 2026-03-10.
4) KV cache warmup smoothing: reduce sensitivity to cache miss spikes when evaluating probe-worthiness. Owner: Lina Chen. Estimate: 5 pts. Due: 2026-03-30.
5) Canary + synthetic load test: create a canary that injects controlled bursts to validate probe behavior before rollout. Owner: SRE Team (lead: Omar Reyes). Estimate: 5 pts. Due: 2026-03-18.
6) Runbook updates: update incident playbook to include quick rollback steps and a checklist for probe-related regressions. Owner: Aisha Khan. Estimate: 2 pts. Due: 2026-03-08.

Current status and next steps:
- Hotfix/Rollback completed and system stable.
- Telemetry PRs merged for basic probe counters (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8235).
- Work in progress: probe backoff design doc in review (Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Probe+Backoff+Design).
- Blocking dependency: need scheduler shared-state refactor (ENG-445121) to implement global probe controller safely.

Acceptance criteria for closure:
- No recurrence of probe-induced tail regressions during a 30-day burn (monitored) while under 2x baseline burstiness for the affected models.
- New telemetry shows probe concurrency per worker <=1 under sustained bursts after backoff enabled.
- Canary tests validate no >10% p95 degradation for mid-length workloads under synthetic bursts.
- Runbook updated and reviewed by SRE and runtime teams.

Open questions / discussion items:
- Should kernel blacklist be adaptive based on observed probe failure reasons (compilation OOM vs. micro-arch mismatch)?
- Is global gating worth the added complexity given the potential for single-controller failure modes?
